title: Colorado AI Act (SB 24-205): Impact Assessment and Reasonable-Care Duty -- In Force Feb 1, 2026
context: 2026-08-14 engine cycle -- Colorado AI Act core obligations in force since Feb 1, 2026; rulemaking and enforcement posture through 2026
body: The Colorado AI Act (Senate Bill 24-205, codified at C.R.S. 6-1-1701 et seq.) imposes a reasonable-care duty on developers and deployers of high-risk artificial-intelligence systems to protect consumers from algorithmic discrimination, and requires developers to complete and document an impact assessment for each high-risk system before it is made available. The obligation became enforceable on February 1, 2026, so the question is no longer whether to prepare -- it is how to evidence the duty after the fact. For a verification-first operator the impact assessment is a measurement document: an honest impact assessment states the known and unknown failure modes of the system, the data it was trained and tested on, the mitigations in place, and the residual risk -- each of which is a claim that should be backed by a measured, independently signed record rather than an assertion. The Council of AI treats the reasonable-care standard as a boundary-monitoring problem: you cannot show you took reasonable care with a model you never measured, and you cannot make that care auditable unless the measurement is signed and reproducible. The posture is monitored containment, not provable isolation -- the impact assessment does not prove the system cannot discriminate, it proves the path from claim to measured behaviour is watched and verifiable. Concretely: (1) every high-risk system under Colorado scope must carry an impact-assessment record keyed to measured pre-deployment behaviour. (2) That record must be independently signed so a regulator or plaintiff can verify the care claim against evidence. (3) The record feeds the Council of AI Containment Incident Index, so a post-deployment divergence from the assessed behaviour is traceable to a boundary event.
